newsitem.title: USA: Big caps in for rough ride in '97 - fund managers.
newsitem.headline: Big caps in for rough ride in '97 - fund managers.

text.p: Popular big-capitalization stocks are likely to retreat in the coming months, managers for growth mutual funds predicted on Thursday.
"1997 is going to be a year of increased volatility for big-cap stocks," said Glenn Fogle, portfolio manager for Twentieth Century Mutual Funds, including Vista, a growth fund.
James Margard, senior equity strategist for Ranier Investment Management, said "the 'Nifty Fifty' will likely decline in coming months".
The managers said that the group -- which includes stocks such as Microsoft Corp, Intel Corp and McDonald's Corp -- will decline in part due to the run-up in prices in recent months.

The widely held stocks have become safe havens for many individual investors, although the notion of safety, defined by individual investors as steady growth, may be illusive in the coming months, they said.

Large-cap stocks, especially ones with sizeable international business, will be vulnerable to macroeconomic conditions, including a stronger dollar, slow growth in Gross Domestic Product, as well as lower earnings growth.
Many analysts have predicted that earnings growth for the S&P 500 will decline over the 1996 level.
And in 1997, big-cap stocks will not match the big gains they captured in the last year and a half.

Fogle said companies such as Tellabs Inc, which makes voice and data equipment used by phone companies, is less vulnerable to international business and macro conditions, and more focused on growing business domestically.

Foster Friess, chairman of Friess Associates, which manages the Brandywine funds, said he is especially bullish on certain technology sectors, including telecommunications switching companies, modem makers, and firms that offer remote video access for teleconferencing.
Elizabeth Bramwell, a longtime money manager and creator of the Bramwell Growth Fund, said the results of the U.S. elections will calm Wall Street in the near term.
She said a Republican-controlled U.S. Congress will push a pro-business stance of lessening regulations, which will please Wall Street investors as well as corporate executives.
The managers were at the Charles Schwab & Co Inc annual Institutional Conference here.
